title: The Hidden Costs of Downtime 2026
gist: Oxford Economics and Splunk surveyed 2,000 executives at Global 2000 companies and put the aggregate cost of cybersecurity-incident-triggered downtime at $600 billion. The report argues outages now ripple into regulatory fines, ransomware payouts, stock-price dips and reputational damage as interconnected digital ecosystems (third-party vendors, cloud providers, autonomous AI agents) multiply points of failure, while AI itself both speeds incident resolution and introduces new failure modes.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics and Splunk frame the aggregate cost of cybersecurity-incident-triggered downtime across surveyed Global 2000 companies as a '$600 billion wake-up call' for boardrooms.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: A $600B aggregate downtime bill signals cybersecurity resilience is now a material line item for enterprise budgets and a factor in operational-risk pricing, not just an IT cost center.
insights.quote: A $600 billion wake-up call, in partnership with Splunk

insights.claim: The findings come from a survey of 2,000 executives at Global 2000 companies conducted by Oxford Economics and Splunk to measure the immediate and long-term effects of downtime caused by cybersecurity incidents.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: A 2,000-executive Global 2000 sample gives the $600B figure and related claims more weight than a niche vendor survey, useful for citing in risk assessments.
insights.quote: Oxford Economics and Splunk captured responses from 2,000 executives from Global 2000 companies to analyse the immediate and long-term effects of downtime triggered by cybersecurity incidents.

themes.theme: Downtime as a Boardroom-Level Business Risk

insights.claim: Downtime from cybersecurity incidents has shifted from being treated as a routine IT headache to being recognized as a boardroom-level crisis for large enterprises.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Investors should expect cybersecurity resilience disclosures and incident response spending to increasingly surface in board-level governance and earnings commentary, not just IT budgets.
insights.quote: Downtime has stopped being just an IT headache and become a boardroom crisis.

insights.claim: A single outage now spreads its financial fallout into multiple distinct channels: regulatory fines, ransomware payouts, stock price declines, and reputational damage.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Modeling downtime risk purely as lost-revenue-per-hour understates exposure; investors should also weight regulatory and equity-price channels when assessing a company's cyber risk.
insights.quote: outages now ripple into regulatory fines, ransomware payouts, stock price dips, and reputational damage.

themes.theme: Expanding Attack Surface From Interconnected Ecosystems

insights.claim: As companies rely more on interconnected digital ecosystems — third-party vendors, cloud providers, and now autonomous AI agents — each new link in that chain becomes an additional point of failure.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Enterprise reliance on third-party vendors, cloud infrastructure, and AI agents is expanding the attack surface faster than it is being secured, a structural tailwind for cybersecurity and resilience vendors.
insights.quote: As organisations lean further into interconnected digital ecosystems — third-party vendors, cloud providers, and now autonomous AI agents — every new link becomes another point of failure

insights.claim: The report examines where outages actually originate across a spectrum ranging from everyday human error to sophisticated cyberattacks, rather than treating cyberattacks as the sole cause of downtime.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Because human error is cited alongside sophisticated attacks as a downtime origin, resilience spending should cover process and training controls, not just technical cyber defenses.
insights.quote: uncover where outages actually originate, from everyday human error to sophisticated cyberattacks

themes.theme: AI's Double-Edged Role in Incident Response

insights.claim: AI is reshaping incident response by helping teams resolve outages faster, but it is simultaneously introducing new failure modes of its own into enterprise systems.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: AI adoption in IT operations is not a pure resilience win; investors evaluating AI-driven ops tooling should weigh the new failure modes it introduces against the speed gains it delivers.
insights.quote: how AI is reshaping the equation, helping teams resolve incidents faster while introducing new failure modes of its own.

insights.claim: The most resilient organizations are moving toward treating downtime as a business risk rather than a technical issue, building what the report calls 'predictive immunity' that distinguishes market leaders from laggards.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Firms that reframe downtime as enterprise risk and invest in predictive capabilities are positioned as the differentiated 'market leaders' the report points to, a lens for evaluating operational-resilience maturity when screening companies.
insights.quote: strategies resilient organisations are using to treat downtime as a business risk and build the kind of predictive immunity that separates market leaders from the rest.
